author: ignatius-of-antioch
fields.title: The Epistles of Ignatius and His Life's Story
fields.subtitle: Seven Letters from the Road to Martyrdom
fields.description: The seven letters of Ignatius of Antioch — written around AD 108 as he was carried under armed guard across Asia Minor to be thrown to the wild beasts at Rome — are the earliest Christian letters we have after the New Testament. In them a bishop on his way to death pleads for the unity of the church, defends the reality of Christ's flesh against those who denied it, calls the Lord's Supper “the medicine of immortality,” and longs to be “the wheat of God.” Five short chapters tell his life and set the stage; then the letters themselves, in J. B. Lightfoot's translation.
fields.attribution: The epistles are public domain, in the translation of J. B. Lightfoot (*The Apostolic Fathers*), from the Christian Classics Ethereal Library — the genuine seven letters (the shorter recension), not the later interpolated or spurious versions. The five life chapters are an original Ochorus composition.

fields.title: Antioch and the God-Bearer
fields.body_html:
In the first century, in the great city of Antioch in Syria, there lived a man who signed his letters with a strange and beautiful name. He was called Ignatius. But when he took up his pen, he wrote himself down another way: Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus — the God-bearer, one who carries God. It is the first thing he tells you about himself, and in the end it may be the truest thing there is to say.

Antioch was no small place. It was one of the largest cities of the Roman world, a crossroads where Greek, Syrian, Jewish, and Roman lives ran together in crowded streets. It was here, the book of Acts records, that the followers of Jesus were first called Christians. So the church Ignatius served was not a young experiment on the edge of things. It stood at one of the great centres of the faith, in a city that had known the gospel since the earliest days, and it needed a shepherd who could hold it together.

That shepherd was Ignatius. He was an early bishop of the church at Antioch — by the old reckoning the successor of a bishop named Evodius — set over the congregation as its overseer and pastor. We do not know the year of his birth. He came into the world somewhere in the mid-first century, in Syria, and the records that might tell us more have not survived. What we have instead is the man himself, in his own words, near the end of his life.

A man at the close of the apostolic age

To understand Ignatius, it helps to feel where he stood in time. He belonged to the generation that came just after the apostles. The men who had walked with Jesus were passing from the earth, or already gone. The eyewitnesses were becoming memories. And the church they had planted now had to learn how to live without them — how to keep the faith whole when the voices that first spoke it had fallen silent.

By long tradition, Ignatius himself was a disciple of the apostle John, and it was said that Peter had a hand in setting him over Antioch. These are old and cherished stories, and they may hold something true; but they are tradition, not established fact, and it is honest to name them so. What is certain is simpler and enough: he was a bishop of the apostolic age, close enough to its beginning to breathe its air, and charged with carrying its faith forward into a harder time.

There is a legend, too, that Ignatius was the little child whom Jesus once took up in his arms and set before the disciples. It is a lovely picture, and later readers were fond of it — but historians reject it, and it is almost certainly not true. We will not pretend it happened. The real Ignatius needs no such ornament.

The meaning of a name

Return, then, to that name he chose to carry: Theophorus, the God-bearer. It was not a boast. In the letters you are about to read, you will find a man who believed, plainly and without drama, that Christ dwelt in him — that a Christian is a place where God has come to live, a vessel bearing something greater than himself. Ignatius did not merely hold this as a doctrine. He was about to prove it with his body.

For this is the shadow that falls across everything he wrote. The letters in this book were not composed at a study desk in peaceful Antioch. They were written on a road, under guard, by a man being carried across the empire to his death. Somewhere in the last years of his life — around the reign of the emperor Trajan — Ignatius was arrested, condemned, and sent to Rome to be thrown to the wild beasts.

Before we walk that road with him, it is worth pausing here, in Antioch, to see him whole: a bishop of one of the first great churches, a man of the generation after the apostles, who called himself the God-bearer and meant it. Everything that follows is the story of how he made good on the name.

fields.title: Condemned to the Beasts
fields.body_html:
We do not know exactly how it began. The arrest of Ignatius left no report, no transcript of a trial, no list of charges we can read today. What we know is the outcome, because he tells us himself: he had been condemned, and he was being taken to Rome to die. He was to be thrown to the wild beasts.

This happened in the reign of the emperor Trajan, who ruled from the end of the first century into the second. Tradition dates the death of Ignatius to around AD 108. It is worth being honest that the date is not certain — the letters are almost the only firsthand source we have, and only one of them carries so much as a day of the month, with no year attached. Some scholars have argued for a later date, even decades later, into the second century. The traditional reckoning of about AD 108, under Trajan, is the one this book will follow; but the reader should know the ground is softer than a single confident number would suggest.

What the letters are, and are not

Here we meet the strange fact that makes this book possible at all. Almost everything we know of Ignatius comes from Ignatius. The seven letters he wrote on his way to Rome are the great source for his life, his mind, and his death. Later writers add a little — Polycarp, who knew him; Irenaeus and Origen and Eusebius, who came after — but the living voice is his own, preserved in these few pages written under sentence of death.

Over the centuries other letters attached themselves to his name: longer, padded-out versions of the genuine ones, and later forgeries he never wrote. Careful study has sorted the true from the false, and modern scholars are agreed on the seven authentic letters that follow in this book. When Ignatius speaks in these pages, it is really him.

So we cannot narrate his arrest as a scene. We do not have the soldiers at the door, the words of the magistrate, the crowd in the square. There exists a later, dramatic account of his martyrdom, but its details are uncertain and much of it appears to have been added by later hands, and we will not dress it up as fact. What we can say is what he lets us see through his own writing — and that, as it turns out, is a great deal.

A sentence that meant Rome

Consider what his sentence actually required. To be thrown to the beasts was a public spectacle, and Rome was where the greatest spectacles were staged. A condemned provincial like Ignatius could be sent the long way to the capital to die before the crowds. That is why this is not a story of a man executed quietly in his own city. His punishment was a journey — hundreds of miles overland, under military guard, from Syria across Asia Minor and on toward Italy and the arena.

It is a cruel arrangement, and Ignatius knew it. Yet it is precisely this long road to death that gave the church its letters. Had he been killed at Antioch, we might have nothing from his hand at all. Instead he had weeks on the road, halting in city after city, meeting Christians who came out to see him, and in those pauses he wrote.

What is most striking is how he understood his sentence. He did not write as a man dragged unwilling to his end, protesting or despairing. He wrote as a man who had found in his condemnation a strange gift. To be carried to Rome to die was, to him, to be carried toward Christ. The chains did not feel to him like defeat. In the chapters ahead you will hear him say astonishing things about them — that he would not have his friends rob him of what lay at the end of the road.

That conviction is his own, formed in his own hour, and we should not flatten it into a rule for everyone. But it is the key to everything he wrote on the way. A man was being taken across the world to be eaten by beasts, and he sat down, again and again, to write letters not about his fear but about the unity of the church, the reality of Christ, and the hope set before him. The road to Rome is where we go next.

fields.title: The Road to Rome, and the Ten Leopards
fields.body_html:
The road ran west and north, out of Syria and across the wide interior of Asia Minor — the land we now call Turkey. Ignatius travelled it on foot and under guard, a prisoner among soldiers, moving from city to city toward the sea and, beyond it, Rome. He was not young, he was condemned, and he was surrounded the whole way by armed men whose task was to deliver him to the beasts.

Of those men he wrote one of his most memorable lines. Far from softening under kind treatment, he said, his guards only grew harsher. He described the whole company in a single bitter image:

From Syria even unto Rome I fight with wild beasts, being bound amid ten leopards, even a company of soldiers, who only wax worse when they are kindly treated.

Ten leopards — that is how it felt to be chained in the midst of them. The picture is exact and unsentimental. Ignatius does not hide the misery of the journey behind pious language. He was a man in real chains, guarded by real and hardened men, and he names it plainly even as he presses on toward what he believed lay at the end.

Received at Smyrna

The journey was not only hardship. As word ran ahead of him, the churches of the region sent people out to meet the famous prisoner. Along the way he was welcomed, encouraged, and cared for by Christians who counted it an honour to stand with a bishop on his way to die.

The great stop was the city of Smyrna, on the Aegean coast. There Ignatius was received by the local church and by messengers from other congregations who had come to see him. Smyrna had its own bishop, a younger man named Polycarp, who would himself die a martyr many years later and whose name is joined to Ignatius’s ever after. It is fair and true to say that Ignatius was received by Polycarp and the church at Smyrna. Beyond that we should be careful: we do not have a record of their meeting word for word, and it would be inventing to imagine the embraces and speeches of a reunion. What we have is better than invention — the letters that came out of that halt.

The letters written on the road

This is the chapter that explains why the book in your hands exists at all. During his pause at Smyrna, and again at his next stop, Ignatius did a remarkable thing for a condemned man. He wrote.

From Smyrna he sent four letters. Three went back to churches whose delegates had come to greet him — the Christians at Ephesus, at Magnesia, and at Tralles — thanking them, warning them, urging them to hold together. The fourth he sent ahead of himself, to the church at Rome, the city he was travelling toward. That letter to the Romans is unlike the others, and we will come to why.

Moving on from Smyrna, Ignatius reached the port of Troas, near the site of ancient Troy, where ships crossed toward Europe. From Troas he wrote three more letters: to the church at Philadelphia, to the church back at Smyrna that had just cared for him, and a personal letter to Polycarp, its bishop. Seven letters in all — four from Smyrna, three from Troas — written in snatched hours along the way to his execution.

Think of what that means. A prisoner being marched across an empire to be thrown to beasts spent his last free weeks not in complaint but in correspondence, pouring out his heart to churches he loved, most of which he had never seen and would never see. He knew he had little time and much to say. So he wrote quickly, urgently, sometimes almost breathlessly, about the things he believed the churches most needed to hear before he was gone.

Those seven letters are the rest of this book. They are not polished treatises composed in safety. They are the words of a dying man, sent out along a hard road, and they have been read and treasured by the church ever since. Before we turn to them, it is worth pausing to hear what was in them — the heart of the message Ignatius was so desperate to leave behind.

fields.title: The Heart of His Letters
fields.body_html:
When you read the seven letters, it helps to know what to listen for. Ignatius wrote in haste, and his thoughts tumble and repeat. But under the urgency, the same few concerns return again and again. Three, above all, run through everything he wrote: the unity of the church, the reality of Christ, and his own longing to reach God through death. Hear these, and you will hear Ignatius.

Unity under the bishop

The theme that presses hardest is unity. Ignatius was terrified that the churches would splinter — that false teachers and rival gatherings would pull the flock apart once the steadying voices of the apostles were gone. Against that danger he called the Christians to gather as one, around their bishop, their elders, and their deacons. Do nothing on your own, he urged, that divides the body; do nothing that belongs to the church without the one set over it. As he wrote to the Smyrnaeans, it was not lawful to do aught of things pertaining to the Church apart from the bishop.

To the same church he gave a line that has echoed down the centuries:

Wheresoever the bishop shall appear, there let the people be; even as where Jesus may be, there is the universal Church.

That phrase, the universal Church, is a small landmark in Christian writing. The word Ignatius actually used was the Greek katholikē — meaning whole, universal, the church everywhere rather than any one congregation. It is the earliest surviving use of that word for the church, and the same Greek word later came into English as catholic. Here it carries no party meaning; it simply names the one whole people of God, wherever they are found.

The reality of Christ, and the medicine of immortality

Ignatius wrote against a specific error. In his day some teachers, later called docetists, claimed that Christ had never truly had a body — that he only seemed to be born, to eat, to suffer, to die. To Ignatius this was a deadly lie. If Christ’s flesh was not real, then his death was not real, and the whole hope of the gospel dissolved into appearance.

So he insisted, over and over, that Jesus was really born, really crucified, really raised. And he tied this to the shared meal of the church, the breaking of bread, which mattered precisely because the flesh of Christ was true. To the Ephesians he described that bread with a famous phrase:

breaking one bread, which is the medicine of immortality and the antidote that we should not die but live for ever in Jesus Christ.

The medicine of immortality — that is how Ignatius thought of the church gathered at its table around a Christ who was truly flesh and truly risen. The unity he pleaded for was not mere organisation. It was a matter of life, of holding fast together to the real Christ who alone could carry them beyond death.

A longing to reach God

The third theme is the strangest and the most personal. Ignatius did not merely accept his coming death; he longed for it. He had come to see his martyrdom as the way he would at last belong wholly to Christ — the road on which he would finally reach God. This is why, as we will see, he begged the Roman Christians not to save him. He feared their kindness more than the beasts.

It is important to hear this rightly. This was Ignatius’s own conviction, formed in his own extremity, as a condemned man already on his way to die. He is not laying down a rule that every Christian should seek death; he is a particular man, in a particular hour, making sense of the end he could no longer avoid, and finding in it not terror but hope. Read as his own, it is one of the most moving things in the early church: a man walking toward the beasts and calling it the beginning of life.

Unity, reality, and the longing for God — carry these three with you. When Ignatius writes about bishops and bread and beasts, he is always, underneath, writing about the one whole church, the one real Christ, and the God he was hurrying to meet.

fields.title: The Wheat of God
fields.body_html:
The road ended where he always knew it would. Ignatius reached Rome, and there he was put to death, thrown to the wild beasts under the emperor Trajan, around AD 108. That is the fact, plainly stated. The church remembered him ever after as a martyr of the apostolic age, one of the first great witnesses to seal his faith with his blood.

Later tradition placed his death in the amphitheatre of Rome, before the crowds who came to watch such spectacles. That setting may well be true, but it is worth saying honestly that the naming of the venue came later; the writers who mention it may have had little to go on beyond Ignatius’s own words. What we can hold with confidence is the core: he died in Rome, given to the beasts, exactly as he had been sentenced and exactly as he had foreseen.

The wheat of God

He had foreseen it, and he had made his peace with it long before — not the grim peace of a man resigned, but something closer to eagerness. In the letter he sent ahead to the Christians at Rome, written while he was still far off on the road, he reached for an image that has never been forgotten. He thought of himself as grain going into the mill:

I am God’s wheat, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts that I may be found pure bread [of Christ].

The teeth that would kill him were, to Ignatius, the millstones that would make him into something offered up and pure. He did not see the arena as the end of him but as the making of him. And so he could write, of the death rushing toward him, the quiet and staggering words:

Now am I beginning to be a disciple.

Not the end of discipleship, but its beginning — as though everything before had been only preparation for this. A lifetime as bishop of Antioch, and he called the hour of his death the first real step of following Christ.

Do not rescue me

There was one thing he feared, and it was not the beasts. He feared that the Christians of Rome, out of love, would use their influence to have his sentence lifted and rob him of the end he longed for. So the letter to the Romans is unlike all the others. It is not a warning against false teaching or a plea for unity. It is a plea for them to let him die. He begged them:

grant me nothing more than that I be poured out a libation to God, while there is still an altar ready.

He asked them to hold their peace, to pray not for his escape but for his strength, to let the altar stand while it still could. It is an extraordinary reversal — a condemned man pleading with his friends not to save his life. We should hear it as his own conviction, in his own extremity, and not as a rule for anyone else. But we cannot mistake how deeply he meant it. To Ignatius, to be delivered would have been the true loss.

Into the letters

And there the life story ends, as his own words end: on the road, still writing, still reaching toward the God he called himself the bearer of. We do not have the scene of his death, and we will not invent one. What we have is what he left — seven letters, written in haste and under guard, by a man who believed that dying for Christ was the beginning of living for him.

Those letters are what follow. You have now met the man: an early bishop of Antioch who called himself the God-bearer, condemned to the beasts, carried across the world to Rome, writing all the way. What he wrote is best heard now in his own voice. Turn the page, and let Ignatius speak for himself.

fields.title: The Epistle to the Ephesians
fields.body_html:
Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus, to the church that has been blessed with greatness through the fullness of God the Father; that was destined before the ages to enjoy, for ever, lasting and unchanging glory, united and chosen through true suffering, by the will of the Father and of Jesus Christ our God; to the church at Ephesus [in Asia], which deserves all congratulation: warmest greetings in Christ Jesus and in blameless joy.

I welcomed in God your much-loved name, which you hold by natural right, [with an upright and good mind], by faith and love in Christ Jesus our Saviour. You are imitators of God, and with your hearts set on fire by the blood of God, you have carried out perfectly the work that comes naturally to you.

For when you heard that I was on my way from Syria, in chains for the sake of the Name and the hope we share, and that I was hoping through your prayers to succeed in fighting the wild beasts in Rome, so that by succeeding I might be able to be a disciple, you were eager to visit me.

So, in God’s name, I have received your whole congregation in the person of Onesimus, whose love is beyond words and who is also your bishop [in the flesh]. I pray that you will love him as Jesus Christ would have you, and that all of you will be like him. For blessed is the One who has graciously given you, as you deserve, such a bishop.

As for my fellow servant Burrhus, who by the will of God is your deacon, blessed in all things, I pray that he may stay with me, to your honour and your bishop’s. And Crocus too, who is worthy of God and of you, and whom I received as a living example of your love for me, has refreshed me in every way. May the Father of Jesus Christ refresh him in the same way, together with Onesimus, Burrhus, Euplus and Fronto. In them I saw all of you with the eyes of love.

May I always have joy in you, if I am worthy of it. So it is right for you in every way to glorify Jesus Christ, who has glorified you, so that, joined together perfectly in one obedience and submitting to your bishop and elders, you may be made holy in all things.

I am not giving you orders as though I were someone important. For even though I am in chains for the Name, I have not yet been made perfect in Jesus Christ. I am only now beginning to be a disciple, and I speak to you as to my fellow students. For I ought to be trained by you for the contest, in faith, in encouragement, in endurance, in patience.

But since love will not let me keep silent about you, I have taken the lead in urging you to run in harmony with the mind of God. For Jesus Christ, our life that cannot be separated from us, is the mind of the Father, just as the bishops appointed throughout the farthest parts of the earth are in the mind of Jesus Christ.

So it is right for you to run in harmony with the mind of your bishop, as indeed you already do. For your honourable body of elders, which is worthy of God, is tuned to the bishop like strings to a lyre. And so in your harmony and united love, Jesus Christ is sung.

And each of you, all together, form yourselves into a choir, so that being in tune and in harmony and taking your note from God, you may sing in unison with one voice through Jesus Christ to the Father. Then He will hear you, and by your good deeds He will recognise you as members of His Son. So it is good for you to live in blameless unity, so that you may always share in God.

For if in a short time I came to know your bishop so closely, not in a human way but in the Spirit, how much more blessed are you who are as closely joined to him as the Church is to Jesus Christ and as Jesus Christ is to the Father, so that everything may be in harmony and unity.

Let no one be deceived. Anyone who is not within the sanctuary lacks the bread [of God]. For if the prayer of one or two has such great power, how much more the prayer of the bishop and of the whole Church.

So whoever does not come to the gathering shows his pride by doing so and has cut himself off, for it is written, God resists the proud. So let us be careful not to resist the bishop, so that by our submission we may give ourselves to God.

And the more a person sees that his bishop is quiet, the more he should respect him. For whoever the Master of the house sends to manage His household, we ought to receive as we would the One who sent him. So it is plain that we ought to regard the bishop as we would the Lord Himself.

Onesimus himself, without being asked, speaks very highly of your good order in God. He says that you all live by the truth and that no heresy has a home among you. In fact, you do not even listen to anyone who speaks of anything except Jesus Christ in truth.

For some people make a habit of peddling the Name with wicked deceit, while doing other things unworthy of God. You must avoid these people as you would wild beasts. They are mad dogs that bite when you are not looking. You must be on your guard against them, for they are hard to cure.

There is only one physician, of flesh and of spirit, born and unborn, God in man, true Life in death, Son of Mary and Son of God, first able to suffer and then beyond suffering, Jesus Christ our Lord.

So let no one deceive you, as indeed you are not deceived, since you belong wholly to God. For when no craving has taken hold of you that has the power to torment you, then you are truly living God’s way. I give myself for you, and I offer myself as a sacrifice for your church, you Ephesians, famous throughout all the ages.

Those who are of the flesh cannot do the things of the Spirit, and those who are of the Spirit cannot do the things of the flesh, just as faith cannot do the things of unbelief, nor unbelief the things of faith. In fact, even the things you do in the flesh are spiritual, for you do everything in Jesus Christ.

But I have heard that certain people came through your city from over there, bringing evil teaching. You did not let them sow their seed among you. You stopped your ears so that you would not take in what they were sowing. For you are stones of a temple, prepared in advance for a building of God the Father. You are hoisted up to the heights by the crane of Jesus Christ, which is the Cross, with the Holy Spirit as the rope. Your faith is your winch, and love is the road that leads up to God.

So you are all travelling companions, carrying your God and your shrine, your Christ and your holy things, dressed from head to foot in the commandments of Jesus Christ. And I too share in the celebration. I am allowed by this letter to keep you company and to rejoice with you that you do not set your love on anything belonging to ordinary human life, but only on God.

And keep praying for the rest of humanity too (for there is hope that they may repent), that they may find God. So let them learn from you, at least from your actions.

When they burst out in anger, be gentle. When they speak proudly, be humble. When they insult you, answer with prayer. When they go astray, stand firm in the faith. When they are fierce, be gentle. And do not be eager to copy them by paying them back.

Let us show that we are their brothers and sisters by our patience. But let us be eager to imitate the Lord, competing with one another to see who can suffer the greater wrong, who can be cheated, who can be treated as nothing, so that no weed of the devil is found among you. Instead, stay in Christ Jesus in all purity and self-control, in body and in spirit.

These are the last times. From now on let us be reverent. Let us fear the patience of God, so that it does not turn into judgment against us. Either let us fear the wrath to come, or let us love the grace that is here now, one or the other, as long as we are found in Christ Jesus and in true life.

Let nothing dazzle your eyes apart from Him. In Him I carry my chains around, my spiritual pearls, in which I long to rise again through your prayer. May I always have a share in your prayer, so that I may be found among those Christians of Ephesus who were always of one mind with the Apostles in the power of Jesus Christ.

I know who I am and to whom I am writing. I am a condemned man; you have received mercy. I am in danger; you are secure.

You are the road travelled by those on their way to die for God. You share in the mysteries with Paul, who was made holy, who was well spoken of, who deserves every honour. When I reach God, I would like to be found walking in his footsteps. In every letter he mentions you in Christ Jesus.

So make every effort to meet together more often to give thanks to God and to glorify Him. For when you meet together often, the powers of Satan are thrown down, and the harm he intends comes to nothing in the harmony of your faith.

There is nothing better than peace, in which every war of things in heaven and on earth is brought to an end.

None of these things is hidden from you if you are perfect in your faith and love toward Jesus Christ. For these are the beginning and the end of life: faith is the beginning and love is the end. When the two are found together, that is God, and everything else that makes for true goodness follows from them.

No one who professes faith keeps on sinning, and no one who has love hates. A tree is known by its fruit, and in the same way those who claim to belong to Christ will be seen by what they do. For the work is not a matter of what we profess now, but of being found in the power of faith to the end.

It is better to be silent and be real than to talk and not be real. Teaching is a fine thing, if the teacher practises what he teaches. Now there is one Teacher, who spoke and it happened. Yes, and even the things He has done in silence are worthy of the Father.

Whoever truly has the word of Jesus is also able to listen to His silence, so that he may be perfect, so that he may act through what he says and be known through his silence.

Nothing is hidden from the Lord; even our secrets are close to Him. So let us do everything knowing that He lives in us, so that we may be His temples and He Himself may be in us as our God. This is how things are, and it will also be made plain before our eyes by the love we rightly have for Him.

Do not be deceived, my brothers and sisters. Those who corrupt families will not inherit the kingdom of God.

If those who do these things in the flesh are put to death, how much more someone who, through evil teaching, corrupts the faith of God for which Jesus Christ was crucified! Such a person, having made himself unclean, will go into the fire that is never put out, and so will anyone who listens to him.

This is why the Lord received ointment on His head: so that He might breathe incorruption into the Church. Do not be anointed with the foul smell of the teaching of the ruler of this world, or he will take you captive and rob you of the life set before you.

Why then do we not all walk wisely, receiving the knowledge of God, which is Jesus Christ? Why do we perish in our foolishness, not recognising the gift of grace the Lord has truly sent?

My spirit is a humble offering for the Cross, which is a stumbling block to unbelievers, but to us salvation and eternal life. Where is the wise man? Where is the debater? Where is the boasting of those who are called clever?

For our God, Jesus the Christ, was conceived in Mary’s womb according to God’s plan, of the seed of David but also of the Holy Spirit. He was born and was baptised so that by His suffering He might make the water clean.

The virginity of Mary and her giving birth were hidden from the ruler of this world, and so was the death of the Lord: three mysteries to be shouted aloud, which were brought about in the silence of God. How, then, were they revealed to the ages?

A star shone in the sky brighter than all the stars. Its light was indescribable, and its strangeness amazed people. All the other stars, with the sun and the moon, gathered like a choir around the star, but the star itself far outshone them all. People were puzzled about where this strange sight, so unlike the others, had come from.

From that time on every kind of magic and every spell was broken, the ignorance that goes with wickedness disappeared, and the ancient kingdom was torn down, when God appeared in human form to bring the new life that lasts forever. What had been completed in God’s plans began to take effect. From then on everything was thrown into turmoil, because the destruction of death had been set in motion.

If Jesus Christ, through your prayer, counts me worthy, and if it is God’s will, in my second letter, which I intend to write to you, I will explain further the plan I have begun to speak about, concerning the new man Jesus Christ. It consists in faith toward Him and love toward Him, in His suffering and resurrection,

especially if the Lord reveals anything to me. Gather together in common, every one of you, each and all, in grace, in one faith and in one Jesus Christ, who in the flesh was descended from David, who is Son of Man and Son of God, so that you obey the bishop and the elders with undivided minds, breaking one bread, which is the medicine of immortality and the antidote that keeps us from dying, so that we live forever in Jesus Christ.

I give myself for you and for those you sent to Smyrna for the honour of God. I am writing to you from there, giving thanks to the Lord, and I love Polycarp as I love you. Remember me, just as I hope Jesus Christ will remember you.

Pray for the church in Syria, from which I am being taken as a prisoner to Rome. I am the very least of the believers there, yet I was counted worthy to be found serving the honour of God. Farewell in God the Father and in Jesus Christ, the hope we share.

fields.title: The Epistle to the Magnesians
fields.body_html:
Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus, to the church that has been blessed through the grace of God the Father in Christ Jesus our Saviour. In Him I greet the church in Magnesia on the Maeander, and I wish her warmest greetings in God the Father and in Jesus Christ.

When I learned how very well ordered your love is in the ways of God, I was glad, and I decided to write to you in the faith of Jesus Christ.

For since I have been counted worthy to bear a most godly name, in these chains that I carry around I sing the praises of the churches. I pray that there may be in them a union of the flesh and of the spirit that belong to Jesus Christ, our never-failing life; a union of faith and of love, which is to be preferred above everything; and, more than all, a union with Jesus and with the Father. In Him, if we patiently endure all the abuse of the ruler of this world and escape it, we will reach God.

I was allowed to see you in the persons of Damas, your godly bishop, your worthy elders Bassus and Apollonius, and my fellow servant the deacon Zotion. May I have joy in him, because he submits to the bishop as to the grace of God, and to the elders as to the law of Jesus Christ.

And it is right for you too not to take advantage of your bishop’s youth, but to give him all respect, as the power of God the Father deserves. I have heard that the holy elders have not taken advantage of how young he appears, but defer to him as to one who is wise in God. Yet they defer not to him, but to the Father of Jesus Christ, the Bishop of all.

So, for the honour of the One who wanted you, it is right for you to obey without pretending. For a person who deceives the bishop he can see is really trying to cheat the other Bishop, who is invisible. In such a case he has to reckon not with flesh but with God, who knows hidden things.

So it is right for us not only to be called Christians, but actually to be Christians. Some people have the bishop’s name on their lips but do everything without him. Such people do not seem to me to have a good conscience, since they do not meet together properly, as commanded.

Everything comes to an end, and these two things, life and death, are set before us together, and each person will go to his own place. It is as though there were two kinds of coins, one of God and one of the world, each stamped with its own image. Unbelievers bear the stamp of this world, and those who are faithful in love bear the stamp of God the Father through Jesus Christ. Unless we freely choose through Him to die and share His suffering, His life is not in us.

Since, then, in the people I have mentioned I saw your whole congregation in faith and embraced them, I urge you: be eager to do everything in godly harmony. Let the bishop preside in the place of God, the elders in the place of the council of the Apostles, and the deacons, who are very dear to me, be entrusted with the service of Jesus Christ, who was with the Father before the ages and appeared at the end of time.

So all of you, take on God’s character and respect one another. Let no one look at his neighbour in a merely human way, but always love one another in Jesus Christ. Let there be nothing among you that could divide you. Be united with the bishop and with those who lead you, as an example and a lesson of incorruptibility.

So just as the Lord did nothing without the Father, [being united with Him], either by Himself or through the Apostles, so you too must do nothing without the bishop and the elders. Do not try to persuade yourselves that something is right for you to do on your own, apart from the others. Instead, let there be one prayer together, one request, one mind, one hope, in love and in blameless joy, which is Jesus Christ, and there is nothing better than Him.

All of you, hurry to come together as to one temple, God, and to one altar, one Jesus Christ, who came from the one Father, is with the One, and returned to the One.

Do not be led astray by strange teachings or by old myths, which are useless. For if we are still living by Judaism to this day, we are admitting that we have not received grace.

For the godly prophets lived according to Christ Jesus. That is why they were persecuted. They were inspired by His grace so that the disobedient might be fully convinced that there is one God, who revealed Himself through Jesus Christ His Son, who is His Word that came out of silence, who pleased in every way the One who sent Him.

Those who had lived by the old practices came to a new hope. They no longer kept the Sabbath, but shaped their lives by the Lord’s day, the day on which our life also rose through Him and through His death, though some deny it. That death is the mystery through which we came to believe, and that is why we endure patiently, so that we may be found disciples of Jesus Christ, our only teacher.

If that is so, how could we possibly live apart from Him? Even the prophets were His disciples through the Spirit and were waiting for Him as their teacher. And that is why the One they rightly waited for, when He came, raised them from the dead.

So let us not be blind to His goodness. For if He were to treat us as we treat Him, we would be lost. So, since we have become His disciples, let us learn to live as Christianity requires. For whoever is called by any other name than this does not belong to God.

So get rid of the bad yeast that has gone stale and sour, and turn to the new yeast, which is Jesus Christ. Be salted in Him, so that none of you goes bad, for you will be tested by your smell.

It is absurd to speak of Jesus Christ and practise Judaism. For Christianity did not put its faith in Judaism; Judaism put its faith in Christianity, in which people of every language have believed and been gathered together to God.

My dear friends, I say these things not because I have heard that any of you think this way. But as one who is less than any of you, I want you to be on your guard early, so that you do not fall into the traps of empty teaching. Be fully convinced about the birth and the suffering and the resurrection, which took place while Pontius Pilate was governor. These things were truly and certainly done by Jesus Christ our hope. May none of you ever be turned away from that hope.

May I have joy in you in everything, if I am worthy. For even though I am in chains, I cannot compare with even one of you who are free. I know that you are not proud, for you have Jesus Christ in you. And when I praise you, I know that it only makes you more embarrassed, as it is written: the righteous man accuses himself.

So make every effort to stand firm in the commands of the Lord and of the Apostles, so that you may prosper in everything you do, in body and spirit, by faith and by love, in the Son and the Father and in the Spirit, in the beginning and in the end, together with your respected bishop, with the beautifully woven spiritual crown of your elders, and with the deacons who walk in God’s ways.

Submit to the bishop and to one another, as Jesus Christ did to the Father [in the flesh], and as the Apostles did to Christ and to the Father, so that there may be union both of flesh and of spirit.

Knowing that you are full of God, I have encouraged you briefly. Remember me in your prayers, that I may reach God. And remember also the church in Syria, of which I am not worthy to be called a member. For I need your united prayer and love in God, so that the church in Syria may be granted refreshment by the dew of your earnest prayer.

The Ephesians in Smyrna greet you. I am writing to you from there. They are here with me for the glory of God, as you are too, and they have comforted me in every way, together with Polycarp, bishop of the Smyrnaeans. All the other churches also greet you in the honour of Jesus Christ. Farewell in godly harmony, and hold on to an unwavering spirit, which is Jesus Christ.

fields.title: The Epistle to the Trallians
fields.body_html:
Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus, to the church loved by God the Father of Jesus Christ: to the holy church in Tralles in Asia, chosen and worthy of God, having peace in flesh and spirit through the suffering of Jesus Christ, who is our hope through our resurrection to Him. I greet this church in the fullness of God, in the apostolic way, and I wish her warmest greetings.

I have learned that your minds are blameless and steady in patience, not out of habit but by nature. Your bishop Polybius told me so. By the will of God and of Jesus Christ he visited me in Smyrna, and he rejoiced with me so much in my chains in Christ Jesus that in him I saw your whole congregation.

So when I received your godly kindness through him, I gave glory to God, because I found that you are imitators of God, just as I had heard.

For when you submit to the bishop as to Jesus Christ, it is clear to me that you are living not by human standards but by Jesus Christ, who died for us, so that by believing in His death you might escape death.

So it is necessary, as you already do, that you do nothing without the bishop. Submit also to the elders, as to the Apostles of Jesus Christ our hope, for if we live in Him, we will also be found in Him.

And those who are deacons of the mysteries of Jesus Christ must also please everyone in every way. For they are not servants of food and drink but servants of the Church of God. So it is right for them to guard against blame as they would against fire.

In the same way let everyone respect the deacons as they would Jesus Christ, just as they should respect the bishop as a picture of the Father, and the elders as God’s council and the band of Apostles. Without these, there is not even anything that can be called a church.

And I am convinced that this is how you think about these matters. For I received the example of your love, and I have it with me, in the person of your bishop. His very bearing is a great lesson, and his gentleness is power. I think even the godless respect him.

Because I love you, I am holding back, though I could write more sharply on his behalf. But I did not think it my place, as a condemned man, to give you orders as though I were an Apostle.

I have many deep thoughts in God, but I keep myself in check, so that I do not perish through boasting. For now I must be all the more afraid, and not listen to those who would puff me up. Those who praise me like this are a whip to me.

For though I long to suffer, I do not know whether I am worthy. The envy of the devil is hidden from many, but against me it fights all the harder. So I need gentleness, by which the ruler of this world is brought to nothing.

Am I not able to write to you about heavenly things? But I am afraid I might harm you, since you are still infants. So bear with me, in case you are not able to take them in and choke on them.

For even I, though I am in chains and can understand heavenly things, the ranks of the angels and the gatherings of the powers, things seen and unseen, am not a disciple yet because of that. For we lack many things, so that we may not lack God.

So I urge you, or rather not I but the love of Jesus Christ urges you: eat only Christian food, and keep away from foreign plants, which is heresy.

For these people even mix poison with Jesus Christ. They deceive others by a show of honesty, like those who give a deadly drug mixed with honeyed wine, so that someone who does not know, suspecting nothing, gladly drinks in death to his ruin.

So be on your guard against such people. And you will be, if you are not proud and if you hold inseparably to [God] Jesus Christ, to the bishop, and to the commands of the Apostles.

Whoever is inside the sanctuary is clean, but whoever is outside the sanctuary is not clean. That is, whoever does anything without the bishop, the elders and the deacons does not have a clean conscience.

Not that I know of anything like this among you. But I am watching over you early, as my beloved ones, because I foresee the traps of the devil. So arm yourselves with gentleness and renew yourselves in faith, which is the flesh of the Lord, and in love, which is the blood of Jesus Christ.

Let none of you hold a grudge against your neighbour. Give the Gentiles no excuse, so that the godly congregation is not slandered because of a few foolish people. For Woe to him through whom My name is slandered for nothing among some.

So close your ears when anyone speaks to you apart from Jesus Christ. He was descended from David, He was the Son of Mary, He was truly born and ate and drank, He was truly persecuted under Pontius Pilate, and He was truly crucified and died, seen by those in heaven, on earth and under the earth.

He was also truly raised from the dead. His Father raised Him, and in the same way His Father will also raise us who believe in Him, in Christ Jesus, without whom we have no true life.

But suppose it were as some godless people, that is, unbelievers, say: that He only appeared to suffer. They themselves are only an appearance! Then why am I in chains? And why do I long to fight the wild beasts? Then I die for nothing. Then I am telling lies about the Lord.

So avoid those wicked offshoots that bear deadly fruit; whoever tastes it dies on the spot. For these people are not the Father’s planting.

If they were, they would be seen to be branches of the Cross, and their fruit would never perish. It is through the Cross that He, by His suffering, invites us, who are His members. A head cannot exist without members, since God promises union, and that union is Himself.

I greet you from Smyrna, together with the churches of God who are here with me. They have refreshed me in every way, in body and in spirit.

My chains, which I carry around for the sake of Jesus Christ, praying that I may reach God, urge you: stay in harmony and in prayer with one another. For it is right for each of you, and especially the elders, to encourage the soul of your bishop, to the honour of the Father [and to the honour] of Jesus Christ and of the Apostles.

I pray that you will listen to me in love, so that what I have written does not become evidence against you. And pray for me too, for I need your love in the mercy of God, so that I may be granted the destiny I long to reach, and not be found to be a failure.

The love of the Smyrnaeans and Ephesians greets you. Remember in your prayers the church in Syria, of which I am not worthy to be called a member, being the very least of them.

Farewell in Jesus Christ. Submit to the bishop as to the commandment, and to the elders likewise. And each of you love one another with an undivided heart.

My spirit is offered up for you, not only now but also when I reach God. For I am still in danger, but the Father is faithful in Jesus Christ to fulfil my prayer and yours. May we be found blameless in Him.

fields.title: The Epistle to the Romans
fields.body_html:
Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus, to the church that has found mercy in the generosity of the Most High Father and of Jesus Christ His only Son; to the church loved and enlightened by the will of the One who willed everything that exists, through faith and love toward Jesus Christ our God; to the church that presides in the region of the Romans, worthy of God, worthy of honour, worthy of congratulation, worthy of praise, worthy of success, worthy in purity, presiding in love, walking in the law of Christ and bearing the Father’s name. I greet this church in the name of Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father. To those who are united in flesh and spirit with every one of His commandments, filled with the grace of God without wavering, and filtered clean of every foreign stain: warmest greetings in Jesus Christ our God, in blamelessness.

In answer to my prayer to God, I have been allowed to see your godly faces, so I have received even more than I asked. For, wearing chains in Christ Jesus, I hope to greet you, if it is God’s will that I be counted worthy to reach the end.

The beginning has gone well, if only I reach the goal, so that I may receive my inheritance without hindrance. For I am afraid of your very love, that it may do me harm. It is easy for you to do what you want, but it is hard for me to reach God unless you spare me.

For I do not want you to please people but to please God, as indeed you do. I will never again have an opportunity like this to reach God, and you, if you stay silent, could never be credited with a nobler work. For if you stay silent and leave me alone, I will be a word of God. But if you love my flesh, I will once again be only a noise.

Give me nothing more than this: to be poured out as an offering to God while there is still an altar ready. Then you can form a choir in love and sing to the Father in Jesus Christ, because God has seen fit to have the bishop of Syria found in the West, having called him from the East. It is good to set from the world toward God, so that I may rise in Him.

You have never begrudged anyone; you have taught others. And my wish is that the lessons you give as teachers will hold good in my case too.

Only pray that I may have strength inside and out, so that I not only say it but also want it, so that I am not only called a Christian but am also found to be one. For if I am found to be one, I can also be called one, and be faithful when I am no longer visible to the world.

Nothing visible is good. For our God Jesus Christ, now that He is in the Father, is seen all the more clearly. The work is not a matter of persuasive words; Christianity is a thing of power whenever it is hated by the world.

I am writing to all the churches, and I want everyone to know, that I am dying for God of my own free will, unless you stop me. I beg you, do not show me kindness at the wrong time. Let me be food for the wild beasts, because through them I can reach God. I am God’s wheat, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts so that I may be found pure bread [of Christ].

Rather, coax the wild beasts so that they become my tomb and leave nothing of my body behind, so that when I have fallen asleep I will not be a burden to anyone. Then I will truly be a disciple of Jesus Christ, when the world no longer sees even my body. Pray to the Lord for me, that through these means I may be found a sacrifice to God.

I do not give you orders as Peter and Paul did. They were Apostles; I am a condemned man. They were free; I am a slave to this very hour. But if I suffer, I will become a freed slave of Jesus Christ, and I will rise free in Him. For now, in my chains, I am learning to give up every desire.

From Syria all the way to Rome I am fighting wild beasts, on land and sea, by night and by day, chained among ten leopards, that is, a company of soldiers, who only get worse when they are treated kindly. Still, through their mistreatment I am becoming more fully a disciple, though that does not make me righteous.

May I have joy in the beasts that have been prepared for me. I pray that I will find them ready. In fact, I will coax them to devour me quickly, and not do as they have done with some, refusing to touch them out of fear. Even if they are unwilling on their own while I am willing, I will force them to it myself.

Bear with me. I know what is good for me. Now I am beginning to be a disciple. May nothing seen or unseen envy me, so that I may reach Jesus Christ. Let fire and cross and struggles with wild beasts come, [cutting and tearing,] the wrenching of bones, the hacking of limbs, the crushing of my whole body, let the cruel tortures of the devil come at me. Only let me reach Jesus Christ.

The farthest ends of the universe will do me no good, nor the kingdoms of this world. It is better for me to die for Jesus Christ than to rule to the farthest ends of the earth. I am looking for Him who died for us; I long for Him who rose again [for our sake].

The pains of a new birth are upon me. Bear with me, brothers and sisters. Do not keep me from living; do not wish for my death. Do not hand over to the world someone who wants to belong to God, and do not tempt him with material things. Let me receive the pure light. When I get there, then I will be a man.

Allow me to imitate the suffering of my God. If anyone has Him within, let him understand what I long for, and let him feel with me, for he knows what is pressing on me.

The ruler of this world wants to tear me to pieces and corrupt my mind away from God. So let none of you who are near help him. Instead, stand on my side, that is, on God’s side. Do not speak of Jesus Christ and at the same time want the world. Do not let envy live among you.

Even if I myself, when I am with you, beg you, do not listen to me. Believe instead what I am writing to you now. [For] I am writing to you while still alive, yet longing to die. My longing has been crucified, and there is no fire of love for material things in me, only living water speaking within me and saying, Come to the Father.

I take no pleasure in the food that perishes or in the pleasures of this life. I want the bread of God, which is the flesh of Christ, who was descended from David; and for drink I want His blood, which is love that never perishes.

I no longer want to live in a merely human way, and that will happen if you want it to. Want it, so that you too may be wanted. I am asking you in a short letter: believe me.

And Jesus Christ will make it clear to you that I am telling the truth, Jesus Christ, the mouth that never errs, through whom the Father has spoken [truly].

Pray for me, that I may reach the goal [through the Holy Spirit]. I am not writing to you in a human way, but according to the mind of God. If I suffer, it will be because you wished it. If I am turned back, it will be because you hated me.

Remember in your prayers the church in Syria, which has God for its shepherd in my place. Jesus Christ alone will be its bishop, He and your love.

As for me, I am ashamed to be called one of them, for I am not worthy, being the very least of them and born out of time. But I have been shown mercy to be someone, if I reach God.

My spirit greets you, and so does the love of the churches that received me in the name of Jesus Christ, not as a mere passer-by. For even the churches that were not on my route went ahead of me from city to city.

I am writing these things to you from Smyrna by the hand of the Ephesians, who deserve all congratulation. Crocus too, a name very dear to me, is with me, along with many others.

As for those who went ahead of me from Syria to Rome for the glory of God, I believe you have been told about them. Let them know that I am near, for they are all worthy of God and of you, and it is right for you to refresh them in every way.

I am writing this to you on the ninth day before the Calends of September. Farewell to the end, in patient waiting for Jesus Christ.

fields.title: The Epistle to the Philadelphians
fields.body_html:
Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus, to the church of God the Father and of Jesus Christ in Philadelphia in Asia, which has found mercy, is firmly established in the harmony of God, and rejoices without wavering in the suffering of our Lord and in His resurrection, being fully assured in all mercy. I greet this church in the blood of Jesus Christ, which is eternal and lasting joy, especially if they are united with the bishop and the elders with him, and with the deacons appointed according to the mind of Jesus Christ, whom He confirmed and established by His Holy Spirit according to His own will.

I have found that your bishop holds the ministry that serves the whole community not by his own doing or through human beings, and not for empty glory, but in the love of God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. And I am amazed at his gentleness.

His silence is more powerful than other people’s talk. For he is in tune with the commandments like a lyre with its strings. So my soul blesses his godly mind, for I have found it good and perfect, and his temper steady and calm, as he lives in all godly patience.

So, as children [of the light] of truth, avoid division and false teaching. Where the shepherd is, follow as sheep.

For many wolves that look trustworthy use deadly pleasures to take captive those who run God’s race. But where you are united, they will find no room.

Keep away from harmful weeds, which Jesus Christ does not grow, because they are not the Father’s planting. Not that I have found division among you, but rather a sifting.

For all who belong to God and to Jesus Christ are with the bishop. And all who repent and come into the unity of the Church will also belong to God, so that they may live according to Jesus Christ. Do not be deceived, my brothers and sisters.

If anyone follows someone who causes a split, he will not inherit the kingdom of God. If anyone walks by strange teaching, he has no share in the suffering of Christ.

So be careful to keep one Eucharist. For there is one flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ and one cup that unites us in His blood; there is one altar, just as there is one bishop, together with the elders and the deacons, my fellow servants. Then whatever you do, you will do it God’s way.

My brothers and sisters, my heart overflows with love for you, and with great joy I watch over your safety. Yet it is not I but Jesus Christ who does so. I wear His chains, and I am all the more afraid because I am not yet made perfect. But your prayer will make me perfect [for God], so that I may reach the inheritance in which I have found mercy, taking refuge in the Gospel as in the flesh of Jesus, and in the Apostles as in the elders of the Church.

And we love the prophets too, because they also pointed to the Gospel in their preaching, set their hope on Him and waited for Him. Believing in Him, they were saved in the unity of Jesus Christ. They are holy people worthy of all love and admiration, approved by Jesus Christ and counted together in the Gospel of the hope we share.

But if anyone presents Judaism to you, do not listen to him. For it is better to hear Christianity from a man who is circumcised than Judaism from one who is not. But if either of them does not speak about Jesus Christ, I regard them as tombstones and graves of the dead, on which only human names are written.

So avoid the wicked tricks and schemes of the ruler of this world, so that you are not crushed by his plans and grow weak in your love. Instead, all of you come together with undivided hearts.

I thank my God that I have a clear conscience in my dealings with you, and no one can boast, in private or in public, that I was a burden to anyone in anything, small or great. And for all among whom I spoke, I pray that they will not turn my words into evidence against themselves.

For even though some people wanted to deceive me in a human way, the spirit is not deceived, because it comes from God. It knows where it comes from and where it is going, and it searches out hidden things. When I was with you, I cried out; I spoke with a loud voice, with God’s own voice: Pay attention to the bishop and the elders and the deacons.

Yet some suspected that I said this because I knew in advance about the division certain people were causing. But He for whom I am in chains is my witness that I did not learn it from any human being. It was the Spirit preaching, saying: Do nothing without the bishop; keep your body as a temple of God; love unity; avoid divisions; be imitators of Jesus Christ, just as He was of His Father.

So I did my part, as a man devoted to unity. But where there is division and anger, God does not live. Now the Lord forgives everyone who repents, if in repenting they return to the unity of God and to the council of the bishop. I trust in the grace of Jesus Christ, who will strike every chain from you. And I urge you:

Do nothing out of rivalry, but act according to Christ’s teaching. For I heard some people saying, If I do not find it in the ancient records, I do not believe it in the Gospel. And when I told them, It is written, they answered, That is the question. But as for me, my records are Jesus Christ. The sacred records are His cross and His death and His resurrection, and the faith that comes through Him. By these I long to be made righteous through your prayers.

The priests were good too, but better is the High Priest who was entrusted with the Holy of Holies. He alone was entrusted with the hidden things of God. He Himself is the door of the Father, through which Abraham and Isaac and Jacob enter, and the Prophets and the Apostles and the whole Church. All of these come together in the unity of God.

But the Gospel has something special: the coming of the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, and His suffering and resurrection. For the beloved Prophets pointed to Him in their preaching, but the Gospel is the completion of immortality. All these things together are good, if you believe through love.

In answer to your prayer and to the tender compassion you have in Christ Jesus, I have been told that the church in Antioch in Syria is at peace. So it is right for you, as a church of God, to appoint a deacon to go there as God’s ambassador, to congratulate them when they are gathered together and to glorify the Name.

Blessed in Jesus Christ is the one who is counted worthy of such a service, and you yourselves will be glorified. If you are willing, it is not impossible for you to do this for the name of God, just as the nearest churches have sent bishops, and others have sent elders and deacons.

Now about Philo the deacon from Cilicia, a man well spoken of, who is now serving me in the word of God, together with Rhaius Agathopus, a chosen man who has followed me from Syria, having said farewell to this present life: they too speak well of you. And I myself thank God for you, because you received them, as I trust the Lord will receive you. But may those who treated them with dishonour be redeemed by the grace of Jesus Christ.

The love of the brothers and sisters in Troas greets you. I am writing to you from there by the hand of Burrhus, who was sent with me by the Ephesians and Smyrnaeans as a sign of honour. The Lord Jesus Christ will honour them, for they have set their hope on Him in flesh and soul and spirit, by faith, love and harmony. Farewell in Christ Jesus, the hope we share.

fields.title: The Epistle to the Smyrnaeans
fields.body_html:
Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus, to the church of God the Father and of Jesus Christ the Beloved, which has been mercifully given every grace, filled with faith and love and lacking no grace, most worthy of reverence and carrying holy treasures; to the church in Smyrna in Asia: warmest greetings in a blameless spirit and in the word of God.

I give glory to Jesus Christ, the God who has given you such wisdom. For I have seen that you are established in unshakable faith, as if nailed to the cross of the Lord Jesus Christ in flesh and spirit, and firmly grounded in love by the blood of Christ. You are fully convinced about our Lord: that He is truly descended from David according to the flesh, but Son of God by God’s will and power; truly born of a virgin; baptised by John so that all righteousness might be fulfilled by Him;

truly nailed to the cross in the flesh for our sake under Pontius Pilate and Herod the tetrarch (and we are the fruit of that most blessed suffering of His), so that through His resurrection He might raise a banner for all the ages, for His saints and faithful people, whether Jews or Gentiles, in the one body of His Church.

For He suffered all these things for our sake [so that we might be saved]. And He truly suffered, just as He truly raised Himself. It was not as some unbelievers say, that He only appeared to suffer. They themselves are only an appearance! And as they think, so it will happen to them: they will be without bodies, like ghosts.

For I know and believe that He was in the flesh even after the resurrection.

When He came to Peter and those with him, He said to them, Take hold of me and touch me, and see that I am not a ghost without a body. Immediately they touched Him and believed, being joined to His flesh and His blood. That is why they despised death; in fact, they were found to be greater than death. And after His resurrection He ate and drank with them as one who has a body, though spiritually He was united with the Father.

I warn you about these things, dear friends, though I know that you already think this way. But I am watching over you early to protect you from wild beasts in human form. Not only should you not welcome such people; if possible, you should not even meet them. Only pray for them, in case they may repent. That is hard, but Jesus Christ, our true life, has power over it.

For if our Lord did these things only in appearance, then I am a prisoner only in appearance. And why then have I handed myself over to death, to fire, to the sword, to wild beasts? But near the sword is near God; among the wild beasts is with God. Only let it be in the name of Jesus Christ, so that we may suffer together with Him. I endure everything because He Himself, who became perfect man, gives me strength.

But some people deny Him out of ignorance, or rather have been denied by Him. They speak up for death rather than for the truth. They have not been persuaded by the prophecies or by the law of Moses, or even to this day by the Gospel or by the sufferings each of us has endured. For they think the same way about us.

For what good is it [to me] if someone praises me but slanders my Lord by not confessing that He had a real body? Whoever does not confess this denies Him completely, and is himself carrying a corpse.

Since they are unbelievers, I have not thought it right to write down their names. Far be it from me even to remember them, until they repent and return to the suffering of Christ, which is our resurrection.

Let no one be deceived. Even the heavenly beings and the glory of the angels and the rulers seen and unseen face judgment if they do not believe in the blood of Christ [who is God]. Whoever can accept this, let him accept it. Let no one be puffed up by his position, for faith and love are everything, and nothing is to be preferred to them.

But look at those who hold strange teaching about the grace of Jesus Christ that has come to us, and see how opposed they are to the mind of God. They have no concern for love: none for the widow, none for the orphan, none for the suffering, none for the prisoner, none for the hungry or thirsty. They stay away from the Eucharist (thanksgiving) and from prayer, because they will not confess that the Eucharist is the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ, the flesh that suffered for our sins and that the Father in His goodness raised up.

So those who speak against the good gift of God perish in their arguing. It would be better for them to have love, so that they too may rise again.

So it is right for you to keep away from such people and not to speak about them, either in private or in public. Instead, pay attention to the Prophets, and especially to the Gospel, in which the suffering is shown to us and the resurrection is completed.

[But] avoid divisions, since they are the beginning of evil. All of you follow your bishop, as Jesus Christ followed the Father, and follow the elders as you would the Apostles. Respect the deacons as you would God’s commandment. Let no one do anything that concerns the Church without the bishop. Let only that Eucharist be considered valid which is held under the bishop or someone he has appointed.

Wherever the bishop appears, let the people be there, just as wherever Jesus is, there is the universal Church. It is not permitted to baptise or to hold a love feast without the bishop. But whatever he approves is also pleasing to God, so that everything you do may be secure and valid.

From now on it is reasonable for us to wake up and be sober, while we [still] have time to repent and turn to God. It is good to acknowledge God and the bishop. Whoever honours the bishop is honoured by God. Whoever does anything without the bishop’s knowledge is serving the devil.

So may everything overflow for you in grace, for you deserve it. You refreshed me in every way, and Jesus Christ will refresh you. Whether I was with you or away, you loved me. May God reward you. If you endure everything for His sake, you will reach Him.

You did well to receive Philo and Rhaius Agathopus, who followed me for the sake of God, as servants of [Christ] God. They too thank the Lord for you, because you refreshed them in every way. You will lose nothing by it.

My spirit is given for you, and so are my chains, which you did not despise and were not ashamed of. Nor will He, who is perfect faithfulness, be ashamed of you: Jesus Christ.

Your prayer has gone out to the church in Antioch in Syria. Coming from there as a prisoner in most godly chains, I greet everyone, though I am not worthy to belong to that church, being the very least of them. By God’s will this was granted to me, not by anything I did, but by God’s grace. I pray that it may be given to me fully, so that through your prayers I may reach God.

So, that your work may be made complete both on earth and in heaven, it is right for your church to appoint, for the honour of God, an ambassador of God to go as far as Syria and congratulate them because they are at peace, have recovered their proper size, and have had their proper body restored to them.

So it seemed right to me that you should send one of your own people with a letter, to join them in giving glory for the calm that by God’s will has come to them, and because through your prayers they were already reaching a safe harbour. Since you are perfect, let your plans also be perfect. For if you want to do good, God is ready to give you the means.

The love of the brothers and sisters in Troas greets you. I am writing to you from there by the hand of Burrhus, whom you sent with me together with your brothers the Ephesians. He has refreshed me in every way. I wish everyone would imitate him, for he is a model of service to God. The grace of God will repay him in everything.

I greet your godly bishop and your respected elders [and] my fellow servants the deacons, and all of you, each one and all together, in the name of Jesus Christ, in His flesh and blood, in His suffering and resurrection, both bodily and spiritual, in the unity of God and of yourselves. Grace, mercy, peace and patience be yours always.

I greet the households of my brothers with their wives and children, and the virgins who are called widows. I bid you farewell in the power of the Father. Philo, who is with me, greets you.

I greet the household of Tavia, and I pray that she may be grounded in faith and love, both bodily and spiritual. I greet Alce, a name very dear to me, the incomparable Daphnus, Eutecnus, and everyone by name. Farewell in the grace of God.

fields.title: The Epistle to Polycarp
fields.body_html:
Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus, to Polycarp, bishop of the church of the Smyrnaeans, or rather, who has God the Father and Jesus Christ as his bishop: warmest greetings.

I welcome your godly mind, which is grounded as if on an immovable rock, and I give great glory to God that I was allowed to see your blameless face.

May I have joy in it in God. I urge you, by the grace with which you are clothed, to press on in your race and to urge everyone to be saved. Do justice to your office with all diligence, in body and in spirit. Care about unity, for there is nothing better. Bear with everyone, as the Lord bears with you. Put up with everyone in love, as you already do.

Give yourself to constant prayer. Ask for more wisdom than you have. Be alert, and do not let your spirit fall asleep. Speak to each person individually, as God does. Carry the weaknesses of everyone, like a perfect athlete. Where the work is harder, the gain is greater.

If you love good students, that earns you no thanks. Rather, bring the most troublesome under control by gentleness. Not every wound is healed by the same ointment. Ease sharp pains with soothing compresses.

Be wise as the serpent in everything and always innocent as the dove. You are made of flesh and spirit for this very reason: so that you may deal kindly with the things you see in front of you. As for the unseen things, pray that they may be revealed to you, so that you lack nothing and overflow with every spiritual gift.

The times need you, as pilots need winds or a storm-tossed sailor needs a harbour, so that they may reach God. Be sober, as God’s athlete. The prize is incorruption and eternal life, of which you too are convinced. In everything I give myself for you, I and my chains, which you loved.

Do not let those who seem trustworthy but teach strange doctrines unsettle you. Stand firm, like an anvil when it is struck. It is the mark of a great athlete to take blows and still win. But above all, we must endure everything for God’s sake, so that He may also endure us.

Be even more diligent than you are. Understand the times. Wait for Him who is above all time, the Eternal, the Invisible, who became visible for our sake; who cannot be touched and cannot suffer, yet suffered for our sake and endured in every way for our sake.

Do not let widows be neglected. After the Lord, you be their protector. Let nothing be done without your approval, and do nothing yourself without God’s approval, as indeed you do not. Stand firm.

Hold meetings more often. Seek out everyone by name.

Do not look down on slaves, whether men or women. But do not let them become proud either. Let them serve all the more faithfully for the glory of God, so that they may receive a better freedom from God. Let them not long to be set free at the church’s expense, or they may turn out to be slaves of desire.

Avoid evil practices, or rather preach against them. Tell my sisters to love the Lord and to be content with their husbands in body and in spirit. In the same way, urge my brothers in the name of Jesus Christ to love their wives, as the Lord loved the Church.

If anyone is able to remain unmarried and chaste in honour of the Lord’s flesh, let him do so without boasting. If he boasts, he is lost. And if he thinks himself greater than the bishop, he is ruined. It is right for men and women who marry to be united with the bishop’s approval, so that the marriage may be according to the Lord and not according to lust. Let everything be done for the honour of God.

Pay attention to the bishop, so that God may pay attention to you. I give myself for those who submit to the bishop, the elders and the deacons. May it be granted to me to have my share with them in the presence of God. Work hard together, struggle together, run together, suffer together, rest together and get up together, as God’s stewards, advisers and servants.

Please the Commander in whose army you serve, from whom you will also receive your pay. Let none of you be found a deserter. Let your baptism stay with you as your shield, your faith as your helmet, your love as your spear, your patience as your armour. Let your good works be your savings, so that you may receive the back pay that is due to you. So be patient with one another in gentleness, as God is with you. May I always have joy in you.

I have been told that through your prayers the church in Antioch in Syria is at peace. So I too have been greatly comforted, since God has taken away my worry, if only through suffering I may reach God, so that through your prayers I may be found a disciple.

It is right for you, most blessed Polycarp, to call together a godly council and choose someone among you who is very dear to you and also eager, who would be fit to be called God’s messenger. Appoint him to go to Syria and glorify your eager love for the glory of God.

A Christian is not his own master; he gives his time to God. This is God’s work, and it will be yours too when you complete it. For I trust in God’s grace that you are ready for a good deed that is fitting for God. Knowing how sincere and eager you are, I have encouraged you in a short letter.

Because I have suddenly had to sail from Troas to Neapolis, as God’s will directs, I have not been able to write to all the churches. So you write to the churches further on, as one who has the mind of God, so that they may do the same thing too. Let those who can send messengers, and let the rest send letters by the people you send, so that you may be glorified by a deed that will always be remembered. This is worthy of you.

I greet everyone by name, especially the wife of Epitropus with her whole household and her children. I greet my dear Attalus. I greet the one who will be appointed to go to Syria. Grace will be with him always, and with Polycarp who sends him.

I bid you farewell always in our God Jesus Christ. Remain in Him, in the unity and care of God. I greet Alce, a name very dear to me. Farewell in the Lord.
